Our research focuses on the solution of data exchange problems, where we draw parallels with well-defined mathematical concepts such as rings and algebraic structures. Given a schema $\mathsf{S}$ and a key function, we can identify a specific class of universal solutions that enable the equivalence of their expanded schemas through the application of key-covered homomorphisms. By examining this concept, we reveal that having a key-covered component does not necessarily guarantee the existence of consistent and unique universal solutions. Nevertheless, under specific conditions - such as the presence of minimal consistent solutions - we find that the key-covered property yields a crucial invariant, enabling the determination of a single, unique solution that satisfies various requirements.

We introduce pyStoNED, a newly developed Python package facilitating seamless interaction with the StoNED framework through its native API. This package complements a recently published C++ implementation of multivariate regression algorithms within the StoNED ecosystem. By providing a Python interface, pyStNED offers a dynamic and expressive environment, making it ideal for scientific computing and data analysis. It also retains the high-performance and reliability characteristics of its C++ counterpart, making it an ideal choice for real-time multivariate regression applications. A comprehensive tutorial is available for pyStoNED on the package's official website, supporting a range of multivariate regression scenarios.

Predictive models such as the Two Higgs Doublet Model offer potential explanations for the lightest neutrino's mass. We investigate how the High Luminosity phase of the LHC and future electron colliders will influence exclusion limits for a specific, well-defined extension of the Two Higgs Doublet Model, featuring light scalars with CP-violating Yukawa interactions. We observe that the LHC will set more stringent limits on the CP-even Yukawa coupling for a scalar mass of 125 GeV than on the CP-odd coupling, with exclusion limits at 125% and 35% their current values. Electron colliders, specifically the International Linear Collider, will set more stringent limits on the CP-odd Yukawa coupling for a scalar mass of 50 GeV than the LHC, with exclusion limits at 240% and 760% their current values. We further analyze how the LHC and future electron colliders are expected to discover the model if its parameters fall within a specific range.

We've developed an innovative few-shot parsing model called FPIO, designed to handle novel sentences with only prototype parsing information. Prototype parsing offers a useful middle ground between fully supervised and weakly supervised parsing, providing explicit category annotations for parse trees. However, even with this information, the process of aligning tokens to latent state variables in the parser is still required. Our FPIO model utilizes prototype parsing features in two distinct ways: prototype category embeddings and coarse alignment information. This allows the model to leverage these features to learn contextual embeddings and initial alignments, significantly outperforming previous few-shot parsing methods when trained on a small dataset of annotated parse trees. Specifically, FPIO achieves superior performance on multiple datasets, surpassing the performance of other models trained on as few as 50 annotated parse trees.

This study investigates the generalizability of the General Audio Visual Regression Model (AVRM) in speech recognition, particularly its performance with diverse datasets, including ones with significant speaker variations and topic shifts. We found that incorporating data from multiple topics and speakers enhances the model's robustness, making it more resilient to changes in speaker contexts and topic expansions. We also examined the AVRM's ability to adapt to novel topics and speakers, and how fine-tuning the model affects its accuracy and stability compared to other training strategies. Additionally, we compared the effectiveness of pre-trained AVRM models, including those designed for speech, speech-visual, and vision-only tasks, in maintaining high performance when faced with unseen speaker and topic variations.

A study was conducted to examine the binary systems of Be-type stars, focusing on short-period cycles that recur (typically between 70 to 180 days) based on data collected from 28 Be stars and 13 normal B-type stars.  The results indicate that Be stars exhibit notably higher frequency oscillations (around 78 seconds) in comparison to the broader range observed (between 90-180 seconds) in normal B-type stars.  A significant distinction was found when the team compared the amplitude levels of these systems, revealing that low-amplitude oscillations (around 5 mmag) in Be stars are notably different from those of normal B-type stars, which have much higher amplitudes (ranging between 10-300 mmag under various conditions).  A distinction based on the presence of binary companions was also identified, as those with other stellar companions exhibit notably higher frequency oscillations (around 90 seconds) in contrast to those with companion OB-type stars and binary systems containing a Be star.  A theoretical model has been proposed that suggests the influence of the binary system's outer critical coalescence, which is linked to the frequency and amplitude of the oscillations, to explain the observed variability.  Ultimately, the research highlights the need for further monitoring of these systems over extended periods using dedicated observing instruments to shed light on the underlying physics of these systems.

Out-of-domain text matching tasks, such as identifying named entities and detecting relation shifts, pose significant challenges for models not trained with such out-of-domain data. In contrast to traditional approaches, which rely on retraining the model with extended training data, we present a more efficient method for addressing these challenges. This method involves using a simple yet effective technique for augmenting the training data, which does not necessitate retraining the model or large quantities of additional data. Furthermore, we subdivide this technique into two distinct components, each capable of handling distinct aspects of out-of-domain data changes, and showcase their individual and combined contributions to models' performance. Notably, this technique has been demonstrated to enhance various models, including fine-tuned BERT and iTN, without the need for further optimization. Moreover, we illustrate its benefits in settings with limited data and widespread linguistic alterations across out-of-domain data, which outperforms the current state-of-the-art models without the advantages of pre-trained data. Additionally, we illustrate its applications in two well-known named entity link disambiguation and relation shift detection datasets, which also outperform the current state-of-the-art models in these domains.

The purpose of this paper is to establish a Faber-Krahn type inequality for the first eigenvalue of the Hermite operator in relation to its extremal properties when considering the Heun equation's coefficients. Specifically, we determine that the optimal geometric configuration for minimal eigenvalue values occurs when the string is taut and uniformly bent.

Deep neural networks often exhibit strong predictive performance but can be difficult to grasp due to their complex nature. In contrast, neural tangent kernels (NTKs) behave much like large, complex neural networks while being conceptually similar to simple models, making them easier to understand. In this report, we explain NTKs in terms of a basic, well-known model, which is a linear regression model with random transformations. By building a random forest, we demonstrate how an NTK behaves similarly to an adaptive model that constantly updates and generalizes effectively, while also being intuitive to comprehend.

The extended Hatano-Nelson chain, consisting of alternating opaqueness and transparency, exhibits near-edge states that amplify an electromagnetic wave. This phenomenon, analogous to the skin effect, reveals that the location of these states isn't solely determined by the level of transparency. By averaging the chain's structure, we shift the edge states towards the center, yet this shift is accompanied by a broader spectrum, affecting the emergence of zero-mode states, that isn't feasible through simple averaging. Consequently, this finding may not translate to systems where the propagation of energy is coupled with non-Hermitian interactions, casting doubts on the reliability of Hermitian approximations in such systems.

Our research focuses on exploring auditory semantics through speech feature manipulation. We reveal that altering the convex mix of vocal traits in a women's speech sample results in distinct perceptions of competence, such as increased confidence in the speaker when enhancing it. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that altering the convex mix of vocal traits affects competence perception to a greater extent when done at a word-level compared to sentence-end position. These findings stress the necessity of accurately mixing vocal characteristics in speech synthesis, especially in applications requiring specific tone of voice.

We present a model in which three Dirac fields serve as stable dark matter, having a hidden supersymmetry that's spontaneously broken. The dark matter stability arises from its isolated nature within a $Z_3$ symmetry while the Dirac fields' mass arises from a Yukawa coupling to a complex scalar field that's charged under $U(1)_{B-L}$. The model's symmetry is complete as it's based on the $SO(10)$ grand unified theory, thus offering a compelling explanation for three neutrino flavors.

This research paper investigates how introducing a fundamental physical limit at the atomic level affects the energy properties of triaxial nuclei. Triaxial nuclei are a type of nuclear state characterized by three distinct symmetries. In this study, we use a modified version of the Strutinsky method to preserve the original energy characteristics of triaxial nuclei. We then apply this modified approach to a theoretical nuclear model and use it to predict the energy patterns of states with a specific amount of angular momentum in nuclei with a minimum measurable length. The research finds that as this minimum limit approaches zero, the energy patterns of the nuclear states regain their original characteristics. Additionally, we identify a relationship between this minimum limit and the changes in nuclear shape. In particular, we observe that as this minimum limit approaches zero, the energy patterns of the nuclear states converge towards a continuous spectrum of energy levels that are separated by the angular momentum.

We provide four feasible quaternary Golay complementary array (GCA), each defined on a different surface of minimal norms, all having the same set of absolute values for their components: $\{0, 1, 2, 3\}$. We explore the feasibility of quaternary GCAs in relation to feasible quaternary partial sum sets of $E_7$-spherical arrays (ESAs).

Recent advancements in change detection using deep networks have shown promising results, mainly focusing on supervised methods which can be resource-intensive and require extensive annotated data sets. To address this, this paper explores the application of a widely accessible, yet underutilized technique - unsupervised change detection using optical and synthetic aperture radar imagery, and assesses its performance compared to supervised methods. Building on deep anomaly detection and feature learning techniques, the proposed unsupervised approach achieves change maps and features using single-date labels. Experimental outcomes using real-world SAR data indicate that the proposed method delivers accurate change detection without relying on data sets like CBSD62 and accurate feature learning.

Utilizing molecular dynamics simulations and the Irving-Kirkwood method, we calculate the viscosity of four non-associating molecular fluids, with their molecules featuring varying numbers of weak non-polar interactions. We determine the ratio of bulk viscosity to shear viscosity for these fluids, modeling their behavior across a wide range of densities and temperatures, with a particular focus on densities between 5 and 30 times their liquid density. To characterize the flow behavior of these fluids, we employ the exponential decay rate of the autocorrelation function of the off-diagonal linear pressure tensor element. Through this analysis, we establish that the flow behavior of these fluids can be accurately characterized by a single exponential decay rate at temperatures corresponding to their 80th percentile, based on a MD simulation dataset involving different molecular models and a broad range of temperatures. Additionally, we observe that the magnitude of this decay rate is directly proportional to the shear stress, allowing us to establish a linear relationship between the shear stress and viscosity. Based on this investigation, we conclude that our density-based viscosity mapping approach can be effectively applied across a broad range of densities, with a particular extension to temperatures spanning a wide range, thanks to the flow behavior characterization.

A novel modification to the $\Lambda$CDM model is introduced as the gravitational constant $G$ fluctuates according to the equation $G=G_0(1+\alpha\sin(\beta\phi)/u^2)$ in a modified quintessence theory, where $\alpha$, $\beta$, and $G_0$ are constants, $\phi$ is the modulated field, and $u$ represents the spatial volume. By convection, this modification introduces a periodic phenomenon in the evolution of the universe, where the universe transitions from a $\Lambda$CDM phase in the past to an inflationary phase in the present and possibly a de Sitter phase in the future. Furthermore, two models, $f(\mathcal{R})$ gravity and $f(G)$ gravity, have been converted into periodic gravity theories, where the latter is represented by the equation $f(G)$=$f(G_0)+(G-G_0)\alpha\sin(\beta\phi)/u^2$. In addition, the effects of periodic modification on cosmological expansion, matter and quintessence energy densities, and the age of the universe have been calculated using an exact solution obtained through a Taylor series approximation. Lastly, the conditions required for the existence of the universe's periodic modification are discussed.

The concept of measuring an observable without directly interacting with it raises intriguing questions about nonlocality and the principles of quantum theory. Traditionally, counterfactual measurements have been assessed within the frameworks of quantum mechanics and quantum information. However, these assessments are often based on specific models and methods. By reevaluating these processes, our aim is to identify universal traits that could be applied to various models without a singular approach. By doing so, we have discovered that counterfactual measurements rely on the independence of measurements - a principle that is consistently violated in the processes commonly studied in quantum information and previously assumed to demonstrate nonlocality. Our unique analysis, in contrast to conventional notions, reveals the intricate connections between counterfactual measurements, measurement independence, nonlocality and Bell nonlocality, thus allowing us to clarify long-standing ambiguities in the field. Furthermore, this insight also enables the redefinition of strong Bell nonlocality and serves as a foundation for future research.

The rapidly growing demand for real-time AI capabilities in devices such as smart speakers and wearables has created a significant challenge in keeping pace with the ever-increasing size and complexity of neural networks. There is, however, an urgent need to develop models that are not only highly accurate but also exceptionally lightweight, allowing them to seamlessly integrate into devices with limited memory and processing power. In an effort to address this issue, researchers have focused on creating real-time AI models with the ability to operate efficiently on devices with limited resources. Our work involves analyzing various lightweight models designed to run on devices with restricted resources and evaluating their performance based on criteria such as memory usage, processing requirements, and accuracy levels. By assessing these factors, we hope to establish guidelines for implementing real-time AI models and provide guidance on their practical application in device hardware and software design.

The cluster expansion for the dimer model on isoradial graphs features orthogonal cluster expansions. Dufresne and Gouery's novel approach to matching clusters term-by-term allows for a rigorous derivation of the dimer model's cluster expansion. This method also enables us to simplify and improve upon a theorem initially established by Bender and Chhaibi. Furthermore, we employ a cluster proof to establish a limit theorem, specifically the convergence of the dimer model's cluster expansion on the torus to a multiple of Ginzburg-Landau's cluster expansion, both involving a specific limit of isoradial graphs.

For multivariate response regression in linear models, the Group Lasso has shown to be an effective tool for variable selection, particularly in dealing with numerous categorical variables or extensive phenotypes that result in numerous dummy variables. However, the original algorithm is not efficient due to its high computational requirements, which hinders its practical application. In response, we have developed a revised, efficient Group Lasso algorithm that relies on the Majorization Maximization (MM) strategy. This approach not only reduces computation time but also provides a more accurate solution compared to the original method. Additionally, we provide a flexible framework that allows the algorithm to accommodate different types of group formations and apply L1- and/or L2-penalties to them. A modified proximal gradient method, facilitated by chunking and caching, underlies the MM algorithm. Through iterative modifications that increase stability and reduce computation, the algorithm efficiently identifies coefficients for numerous real-world datasets, outperforming the original Group Lasso and other state-of-the-art algorithms like group lasso with iterative optimization (GLOI) and the blockwise Correlation-based penalty (BCP). Consequently, the new algorithm has substantial potential for variable selection in high-dimensional regression with categorical or phenotypic data.

T-Visor is an open-source virtualization platform developed with the capability of running multiple thread-level parallelism (TLP) hardware schedulers. By leveraging this capability, T-Visor's embedded virtualization scheduler (EVS) is able to effectively manage and utilize various hardware resources to fulfill the unique and multiple real-time needs of embedded systems. However, EVS still has limitations when employing multi-core hardware due to the ineffectiveness of TLP hardware schedulers in managing context switches. Therefore, a new scheduling framework, called SEVS, was introduced to utilize available hardware resources, such as function-level parallelism (FLP) and TLP hardware schedulers, to efficiently create multiple context-aware scheduling groups. These groups can efficiently utilize all available hardware resources, including those from multiple context switches, to schedule various embedded systems with diverse real-time requirements, such as hard, soft, and feaature-based real-time systems, while achieving new benchmarks in performance and energy efficiency compared to contemporary scheduling methods.

A novel method of image stitching in panoramic formats without rotational limitations is presented, utilizing a pair of IMUs to track optical axis angular displacement between captured images. On a standard smartphone, this method enables efficient and precise calibration, as well as full 360-degree imaging without the need for rotating the device. Although non-rotationary imaging was initially designed for 360-degree video creation, our method also addresses calibration challenges in panoramic imaging. Key advantages of our method include minimal additional hardware requirements, alongside reduced power consumption, battery drain, and storage needs. Notably, this method does not require a dedicated lens or a high-quality camera, but rather utilizes at least one movable camera to perform calibration. Using a dataset with over 1000 images, our method successfully achieves accurate calibration in panoramic formats with an average calibration error of less than 0.5 degrees.

Research on chaotic systems, particularly those exhibiting unexpected internal variations, has revealed unique internal equilibrium states. We've extended our understanding of these states by documenting their presence within networks of oscillators that are either weak or absent in nature. Our investigation also uncovered how these internal equilibrium states are affected by differences in variability among individual oscillators within these networks. Additionally, as a practical application, we've successfully created and maintained these internal equilibrium states within networks of physical systems, specifically consisting of pendulums and magnetic spin oscillators, by fine-tuning their connections and magnetic interactions.

One of the significant advantages of learning-based approaches in nonlinear control theory is their ability to develop efficient, data-driven controllers for complex nonlinear systems. However, it's crucial to consider the potential uncertainties in the system dynamics, which could impact the effectiveness of the learned controller. By adding constraints to the likelihood noise in the dynamics model, we can assess the robustness of the learned controller. In this study, we demonstrate that enforcing a lower bound on the likelihood noise in the dynamics, as learned through sequential Monte-Carlo techniques, significantly improves the robustness of the learned controller. We also observe that such a constraint has a natural interpretation within the system's parameter space, which simplifies the implementation in comparison to direct control approaches. We utilize this method to improve the robustness of a learned trajectory generator in a six-degree-of-freedom flight simulator.

For any finite dimensionally directed quiver Q, we define a family of algebras, denoted S(Q, R), that originate from the matrix or tensor algebra on R, a commutative ring. These algebras will serve as the target of extensions derived from temporary quivers and unifying the foundations of slice algebras under matrix and tensor algebra premises. Furthermore, as Q is unitary, the algebras S(Q, R) are speculatively isomorphic to the algebra P(Q, Q^T, R), which is generated by the tensor product of Q and its transpose quiver Q^T over the ring R.

We've discovered that near the center of a random tensor network, a reflected version of the R'enyi spectrum appears, comprising eigenvalues that are essentially their mirror images. These reflected eigenvalues exhibit a scaling behavior more similar to the percolation threshold than the centerpoint, suggesting that the reflected spectrum could serve as a more reliable indicator of the network's bonding threshold. Additionally, we've developed a theoretical model aimed at comprehending the reflected spectrum's emergence.

Building on the concept of probability of persistence for individual dynamical systems, we now explore its application in a collective context - large sets of systems where each member is dynamically interacting with its surroundings. In these complex scenarios, a system's behavior can be influenced by various parameters such as the size of the surrounding area, the rate at which these systems evolve, and dynamic similarities among them. Through mathematical analysis, we find that probability of persistence for extensive collections of systems follows distinct patterns depending on the dimension of phase space and the rate of system evolution. These findings are supplemented by numerical simulations, offering insights into how these results might be useful in understanding and predicting collective behavior in large sets of systems.

We've developed a comprehensive method to analyze the structural components of parameter space for quadratic diffeomorphisms, focusing initially on the generalized H\'{e}non map. By employing a novel extension of Morse-Levine theory, we demonstrate that periodic orbits create singularities in the space, leading to the formation of holes. The interconnection of these orbits in parameter space can be determined through the application of homology and homotopy theories. The results obtained from simple parameterizations reveal that the H\'{e}non map possesses an infinite number of disconnected components, a finding that supports our analytical predictions. This approach holds the potential to be generalized to other families of maps when fully developed.

Holonomy in gauge theory is well understood as a path-transport operation in the associated Hilbert space, but a similar approach in gravity is highly complex. Introducing a discrete metric with holonomy allows for the creation of a path-transport operation in the Hilbert space, but it was considered less effective than gauge theory holonomy. A new research paper proposes a different metric with holonomy that exhibits improved properties. This metric can be represented by a random tensor on a lattice, where each point determines the connection matrix at that location. Additionally, the paper discusses the challenges of defining holonomy in gravity and provides potential future applications.

By utilizing local limits for binomial and Poisson distributions, we demonstrate the asymptotic behavior of cumulative distributions for variables related to the largest or smallest parts in samples of size $n$. The asymptotic expressions for these cumulative distributions are presented in a explicit form. It's further established that the sums of squares of standardized central binomial coefficients converge unconditionally to a normal distribution as $n$ approaches infinity, and a local limit is established for the distribution of these central binomial coefficients. An exact, closed-form expression for the error in approximating the binomial distribution using Laplace's method is derived and shows that this error is of the order $n^{-4}$, with a negative $n$-dependent constant in the exponent for a specific subset of values.

The existing tunneling time literature has a dual model which poses challenges in relating it to the quantum system's fluctuations. To address this, a new tunneling time model, based on the quantum system's spin fluctuations, has been developed. This model is without ambiguities and provides a well-defined tunneling time. The quantum system's spin fluctuations are characterized by the quantum-darwin term in the interaction Hamiltonian and by the fact that the spin operator does not commute with the Hamiltonian, which leads to the spin's reduced density matrix. The quantum system's tunneling is described by the tunneling coupling operator, which is part of the out-off-diagonal term in the density matrix. The new tunneling time (ATT) is given by the quantum-darwin term in the tunneling coupling operator. The existence of ATT was demonstrated by a theoretical analysis of a spin-1/2 quantum system, which showed that ATT can be used to describe the quantum-darwin term in the system's tunneling. The theoretical analysis also provides a new understanding of ATT in terms of spin fluctuations. The model for ATT is a fresh and highly effective approach to measuring tunneling times, which can be applied to a variety of quantum systems.

Our approach enables the systematic calculation of relativistic corrections to observables associated with P-wave charmonia mesons, including $J/P$ and $D_{J/L}$, via relativistic moment methods. This allows us to computationally assess corrections in specific matrix elements related to $J/P$ and $D_{J/L}$, including $k^6$-order terms, to understand how they impact state masses, decay constants, and transition amplitudes between states. Notably, these P-wave states are primarily composed of $1p$-waves, making it feasible to resum Lattice data in regions where lattice artifacts are prevalent beyond $k^2m_{\pi}$-corrections. Our findings include detailed analysis of several important processes involving these states: $J/P$ to $J'/P'$ transitions, $C$-conserving $D_{0}/D_{L}$ conversions, and $C$-changing $D_{J}/D_{L}$ conversions. Relativistic corrections to these amplitudes were found to be significant, up to 100%, and as such, have a substantial impact on state decay constants and transition amplitudes between states. This emphasizes the necessity of incorporating relativistic corrections in P-wave charmonium calculations to obtain accurate results.

We investigate Ramsey interferometry involving quantum systems with linear dependencies, using Bose-Eisen condensates as an example. To enhance the method's precision, we implement an exact, multi-mode quantum state preparation technique based on extensive computer simulations. This involves generating multiple entangled states in a linear chain and utilizing a system of three connected bosons to demonstrate improved performance. Our results indicate that utilizing nonlinear Hadamard gates enables the method to achieve the quantum limit of measurement accuracy, and these gates can be approximated precisely using interacting Bose-Einstein condensate systems. Additionally, we demonstrate that the method remains robust against various types of disturbance and errors, and propose a realistic implementation of the technique using engineered quantum connections.

Building upon our previous research in arXiv:2103.02755, we delve deeper into the concept of Lagrangian meromorphic opers in relation to their connection to deformations of the Bernevig-Hanson-Lam (BHL) theory. Notably, we demonstrate that the BHL theory can be represented as a specific case of the extended BMS charges, whose degeneracies in the vacuum states are linked to the characteristics of "soft news" and Schwarzian modes. Furthermore, we explore the broader context of degeneracies in the context of relative BMS charges and demonstrate that they satisfy a finite-dimensional Lie algebra structure.

Ensemble method fulfillment in Neural Network training involves generating diverse training data samples to prompt NN exploration of a broader space, thereby enhancing generalization capabilities. To accomplish this goal, we've developed an innovative approach, Ensemble Covering Transformation, which creates a diverse set of transformations for training samples. By utilizing these transformations, the ECT method significantly raises classification precision compared to conventional methods and showcases excellent performance on both artificial and real-world classification problems. Its implementation also reflects clarity and moderation in terms of computational resources required. Additionally, we've explored the theoretical underpinnings of the ECT method, which we've discovered involves generating a covering set of transformations to prompt NN exploration of a substantial space. While there exist numerous challenges in obtaining an exhaustive transformation cover, the ECT method has shown promising results on complex classification problems.

We have derived a local finite recipe for obtaining generalized connections from any metric with $Ric=0$, including both Riemannian and pseudo-Riemannian varieties of any dimension greater than one. Unfortunately, this method doesn't lead to global recipes in general, although it works for all cases in two dimensions. When a metric is flat, our recipe becomes quite straightforward, involving just one step: introducing a single condition to select one specific generalized connection. Our recipe also works when a metric is conformally flat, requiring only minor adjustments. We have further demonstrated that certain generalized connections derived from Ricci flat metrics share key properties with the original Riemannian connection, while also establishing a relationship between the curvature of these connections and the vanishing of the Weyl tensor.

We establish a concept of complete mapping within the scope of polynomial functions over finite fields in order to expedite the process of testing bijections between finite fields and algebraic tori over arbitrary field closures, specifically algebraic field extensions. Furthermore, through the concept of the trace of polynomial functions, we develop an innovative strategy to identify all bijections between finite fields and algebraic tori over algebraic field extensions by solving a specific problem: determining the count of complete mappings of a polynomial function over a finite field. This problem is then solved through the integration of multiple advanced mathematical theories, including the Chebotarev density theorem for dynamical systems, the boundedness theorem for diophantine systems, the Frobenius determinant, and the standard material from number theory, the arithmetic of algebraic tori, and the expounding upon Chowla and Kneser's conjecture, specifically a version tailored for finite fields and polynomial functions.

Visual inspection is often regarded as inaccurate due to its vulnerability to errors, yet it remains a widely used method for intestinal parasite identification. We applied deep learning techniques to examine the effectiveness of human visual inspection in diagnosing intestinal parasites by analyzing images of stool samples. The study found that combining human visual inspection with a deep learning system results in superior diagnostic performance compared to relying solely on human judgment, achieving high levels of specificity (99%) while maintaining a comparable level of sensitivity (95-96%) in combination with the human visual inspection.

This paper uses the variational iteration method to solve nonlinear Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equations, which involve an integro-differential equation with unknown parameters. By constructing suitable guessing functions, we can build an accurate iterative correction term and thereby implicitly obtain an approximate solution. Moreover, an important feature of this method is its ability to provide a straightforward criterion for determining the necessity and sufficiency of the approximate solution we obtain. In this particular example, we can determine the necessity of the solution by examining a set of six straightforward conditions, and although the set of necessity conditions is not minimal, the solution turns out to be exact when all conditions are satisfied.

This study introduces a control method for a quadcopter system subjected to unpredictable and variable disturbances. By integrating the Genetic Filter into a backstepping-based control design, the system's stability and robustness can be significantly improved. The Genetic Filter serves as an adaptive dynamic surface controller, accurately calculating and canceling out the unknown disturbance forces and moments. Consequently, it enables the achievement of stable and precise vertical takeoff and landing, as well as robust trajectory tracking, in the presence of constant or random disturbances. Simulation tests using a hypothetical quadcopter model validate the efficacy of the proposed algorithm.

The KN sigma term, expressed as $\langle p \rangle$, plays a crucial role in understanding nuclear physics, but its precise value remains elusive. This paper explores the possibility of calculating $\langle p \rangle$ through two routes. Firstly, by using lattice QCD with dynamical quarks, it is possible to compute $\langle p \rangle$. Secondly, an estimate can be made based on the difference between the nucleon-pion correlation function and that of the pion-nucleon correlation function, both of which can be studied using finite-volume lattice simulations. Our findings from using domain wall fermions and two flavours of dynamical quarks are presented. Specifically, we have shown that $m_\pi$ and the nucleon mass $m_N$ are both dependent on the lattice spacing $a$ and the lattice volume $V$. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that $m_N$ in units of the lattice spacing $a$ is a linear combination of $\log \frac{V}{a}$ and an artificial dependence on the hinge applied boundary conditions at infinity. Our results suggest that when working at a specific volume $V$ and with a more accurately known $m_\pi$, we are able to compute the dependence of $m_N$ on the lattice spacing $a$ through a nucleon propagator in three-dimensional space. Our proposed methods for calculating $m_N$ and $\langle p \pi\rangle$ are yet to be applied in simulations conducted at infinitesimal lattice spac

In line with the goal of maintaining the CMS Open Data initiative, the following presentation outlines the upgrades to the CMS detector's silicon pixel detector undertaken in 2016. The upgrades enhanced the detector's capabilities, including increasing its acceptance of minimum-ionizing particles by 30%. Following these upgrades, a comprehensive dataset was collected from proton-proton collisions at a record-breaking 136.6 fb^-1 cross-sectional density at 13 TeV collision energy between 2016 and 2018. The following presentation demonstrates the significance of these upgrades in high-energy physics research by highlighting four studies on the CMS pixel detector's performance. The first study involved analyzing data from the CMS detector to measure the long-term relative change in the detector's resistance after the upgrades. The second study focused on investigating four physical damage modes to the detector's analog front-end readout chip. The third study utilized data from the CMS to measure the lifetime of the b-quark by analyzing exclusive b-hadron semileptonic decay events. The fourth and final presentation details the CMS detector's reliability during data collection and in-operation calibration of the analog front-end readout chip.

Using the multi-color dataset from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program, we have developed a technique for identifying and removing the dominant source of point source contamination in galactic identifications, which has been achieved through photometric mapping of the galaxy's extended structure. By applying this method, we re-evaluated the galaxy identifications in the STORM field for 413 active galactic nuclei within a redshift range of 0.3 to 4.3. Following the contamination removal, we noticed a variation in the accuracy of AGN host galaxy classification between different redshift intervals, with a precision of 75% at z= 0.3-0.5, 65% at z= 0.5-0.75, and 35% at z= 0.75-4.3. We found that the precision for galaxies with a redshift above 1.0 is around 50%. We then separated the galaxies into two categories, based on their orientation (kpc), and found that the elliptical and compact galaxies have higher accuracy (up to 90%) at lower redshifts (z < 0.7). We discovered that galaxies with a disk component and those that are kpc-distant from the active region have higher accuracy (up to 80%) at a redshift range of 0.5-0.75. A comprehensive approach has been adopted to investigate the impact of neutron-proton correlation in dense nuclear matter on the thickness of the outer neutron layer in certain isospin-asymmetric nuclei. By utilizing the phenomenological approach, researchers have determined that the neutron skin thickness in certain isospin-asymmetric nuclei is directly influenced by the amplitude of neutron-proton short-range correlations, with a reported amplitude of approximately 0.4 and a resulting skin thickness of about 0.18 femtometers. However, recent studies have suggested that the high momentum components of this correlation, dominated by the tensor force, significantly contribute to the amplitude, leading to a re-evaluation to assess the role of tensor forces in this correlation. By incorporating more realistic potentials that incorporate tensor forces and studying the variation of the density dependence within the density range, researchers have determined that the tensor force's influence on the amplitude results in a reduced thickness of about 0.13 femtometers.

This paper presents an alternative representation of RGB images using complex-valued scaling. By viewing an image as a continuous function with three values at different colors, we can translate this information into a continuous, complex-valued surface where red, green, and blue components correspond to specific imaginary components at different points in space. This approach leads to unique properties, including invariance to hue shifts and the preservation of the relationships between color channels. We demonstrate that the proposed representation facilitates smoother image translation and rotation, which has significant implications for our understanding of the geometry of image colors. Experimental results indicate that our formulation results in lower optic flow errors compared to existing methods, such as SIENAX and FAST, especially in complex scenarios involving VLR transformations.

The geometrical scaling of gluon distribution in nuclei, observed in DIS experiments, is also present in predictions of QGSII and QGSJET II II models for cosmic ray interactions with air. These models incorporate the LPM effect and Hockney's technique for diffusion, contributing to understanding diffusion and correlation phenomena in extended systems. By reproducing calculated gluon distributions in nuclei within the QGSII model, a functional form is derived, which in return helps understand the geometrical scaling observed in nuclei, while indicating that similar geometrical scaling can occur in proton structure as well. Additionally, correspondence is found between predictions of both QGSII and QGSJET II II models for gluon distributions in nuclei and those of HAJDUQCD, a Monte Carlo model describing nuclei and quark-gluon plasma in jets.

This study introduces a pioneering approach to tackle the challenges of early galaxy star and planet formation being influenced by the uncertainties surrounding the core-collapse supernova (CCSN) mechanism. A groundbreaking method is developed to statistically sample the mass distribution of CCSN progenitors 14 billion years ago by considering the enrichment of heavy elements in the early galaxy. To verify the new approach, it is applied to two galaxies with the youngest populations, including SMC and RMC136. The method dynamically identifies probabilistic mass ranges for CCSN progenitors at each time and accounts for uncertainties in energy deposition, which aligns with recent observations and simulations of explosive nitrogen production via the rapid neutron capture element process (r-process). Moreover, by analyzing the mass distribution of CCSN progenitors, it becomes apparent that CCSN energy has declined over time. Consequently, fewer energy was released from CC SNe in the early galaxy, leading to reduced supernova influence on the formation of the early galaxy's heavy elements. To account for this, it is proposed that CCSN energy regulation be incorporated into future CC SNe simulations to ensure they are consistent with early galaxy mass and metallicity patterns.

The performance of machine learning models in predictive tasks can be impacted by the complexity of their characteristics, particularly when using generated predictors. To assess model reliability in terms of predictive performance and stability, we investigate a particular metric known as the Levenshtein distance between predictive outputs. By defining this distance, we can evaluate a model's stability in response to added synthetic predictors, which provides insight into its robustness and predictive performance. Ultimately, our study demonstrates that a measure of model stability can serve as an indicator of a model's dependence on training data coordinates, thereby offering a quantitative assessment of model reliability.

Variational quantum models, defined as quantum circuits for sampling probability distributions, have the potential to serve as a foundation for quantum machine learning. Following a review of the underlying principles and available literature, we assess the current state of two types of probability output, specifically, the computational feasibility of utilizing gradient-based optimization methods in relation to output energies and output probabilities. Our analysis suggests that using output energies may facilitate faster convergence but compromises the model's scalability, whereas using output probabilities is more feasible in terms of scalability but requires further research to improve convergence. Additionally, we propose certain circuit modifications designed to facilitate output energies and make variational quantum models more suitable for classification tasks. Our findings are grounded in experimental results obtained from various applications and datasets, which demonstrate the efficacy of variational quantum models using output energies, particularly in chemistry-related tasks.

Researchers have thoroughly studied warped product submanifolds in various spaces, specifically in Sasakian manifolds. Specifically, they have investigated pointwise semi-slant submanifolds in these spaces. This paper will explore a new type of submanifold in Sasakian manifolds, namely, a semi-slant submanifold, where both the foliation and the direct sum component are semi-slant. Unique to this submanifold is that its leaves may not be geodesic. Preliminary results indicate that semi-slant submanifolds in these spaces are particularly diverse. In fact, they can be either or a combination of a geodesic product of a Sasakian manifold and a manifold that is not geodesic, a Lagrangian or semi-slant immersion, or a combination of these. Additionally, the paper demonstrates that there exist semi-slant submanifolds in these spaces that are not warped product.

The Large Underground Xenon (LUX) Low Background Dark Matter (LUDM) experiment has a single photo-detection system that uses 76 cm in diameter and high purity silicon sensors to cover 125 cm in diameter of its drum-shaped detector. As the experiment doesn't use traditional light-detection technology commonly found in other xenon experiments, the focus is on analyzing the detector's response to novel neutrino interactions. Notably, the LUX-LXe experiment has generated significant interest with the public due to its CEvNS analysis which was published in Nature in 2020. As part of this work, researchers are developing an advanced readout system to characterize NEUSS's (New Enhanced Ultra-sensitive Silicon) sensor dependence on light intensity under high purity xenon layers. Additionally, the LUX-LXe experiment will investigate CEvNS using BECCALIB-calibrated BECCALIB (Boron-Neon Charge Calculation Library) and compare its findings to LUX-LXe's existing CEvNS analysis which was published in Physical Review Letters in 2020. A detailed protocol outlines experimental and analytical procedures for characterizing NEUSS under pure xenon layers, exposing it to controlled light intensities, and cross-referencing the results with established technology-based light-detection systems such as PMT (Photomultiplier Tube) and SiPM (Silicon Photomultiplier), which are commonly used in other xenon light-detection technology. Our investigation focuses on the steady-state circulation of active-dimer mixtures, specifically composed of stick dimers capable of mechanical torque and various steric interactions with a passive solvent. Through in silico analysis, we determine that these stick dimers travel in a spiral pattern when driven by an external force and report this finding's similarity to vehicle motion governed by wheel torque. To elucidate the impact of the dimer's structure on steering dynamics, we explore adaptations, such as modifying the geometry of the stick dimer to a rod dimer, and investigating the influence of car wheel replacement with a track on a theoretical vehicle model to gain deeper understanding and insight into active matter dynamics and its topological classification.

The investigation into chirality characteristics of quantum Hall devices based on moiré patterns consisting of WSe$_2$/MoSe$_2$ semiconductors involves numerical resolution of a lattice model via the time-dependent density matrix method and subsequent nonlinear transport theory application. Calculated results for $
u = 2/7$ reveal both forward and reverse chiral modes within the $
u = 2/7$ moiré state at low temperatures, unlike the scenario at $
u = 2/9$ where only the $
u = 2/7$ edge state exhibits direction-dependent conductance. Furthermore, a developed theoretical framework predicts that, due to inter-valley coupling, a conventional chiral edge current will maintain equilibrium when subjected to a voltage bias, thus preventing the generation of a thermal gradient between contacts that would lead to heat flow in a moiré superstructure. Last, an experiment is proposed that can distinguish between the two proposed mechanisms responsible for the observed chiral modes, one of which is grounded in the moiré superstructure's symmetry rather than the conventional spin or sublattice chirality.

Our research explores the investigation of epidemics on complex networks with various characteristics. Traditionally, studies of this kind often impose restrictive assumptions on network structure, which can be overly constricting and limit the scope of actionable insights for public health policies. In our work, we extend the framework of the contact graph model by relaxing a key structural constraint, allowing us to analyze a broader class of networks, including those that are not inherently symmetric. This relaxation leads to the emergence of two novel mathematical inequalities, which we have chosen to represent symmetrically for analytical simplicity. These inequalities describe relaxation times in terms of energy differences within and between communities, providing a framework for generalised mean field approximation and offering practical recommendations for reducing relaxation times through targeted network interventions. Our findings are demonstrated to be consistent with existing theories on networks with well-defined hierarchical structures and are verified against empirical data on COVID-19 outbreak dynamics across various countries and organizations.

In evaluating the performance of CMB estimators, we're particularly concerned with how they'll be applied to real-world data, where their characteristics aren't always accounted for in simulation environments. This study investigates the impact of high-point sources on bias introduction, particularly in relation to cross-spatial correlation estimators. We analyze two scenarios: first, where the sources' angular distributions are even and second, where they're not. Using these scenarios, we assess the error distribution in reconstructed CMB maps generated by contaminated data. Given that traditional estimators are unreliable when confronted with high-point sources, we explore the potential of using an adaptive weighting strategy to mitigate their influence. Our results demonstrate that this approach significantly reduces the impact of bias, with no corresponding improvement in variance, thus highlighting the value of adaptive weighting in CMB estimator applications. Ultimately, this research aims to contribute an understanding of estimator limitations and potential solutions to improve CMB estimator performance.

This study suggests a task-based approach to instructional design, incorporating pedagogy and pragmatism. Initially, we examine learning through the lens of social and social-cognitive frameworks, finding that task-based instruction fits well within this perspective. Next, we identify and describe a set of core tasks for languages, drawing from an existing framework by Herron and Shieh (2001), and later adapted by Newman and Newman (2001). Their task sets were influenced by the work of Herron and Shieh (2001), which categorized learning tasks into categories such as'Able' and 'Not Able' tasks. We build upon this categorization system, incorporating new tasks like 'Explain', and combining 'Able' and 'Not Able' tasks under the heading of 'Practical' tasks. We propose that Task-Based Instruction (TBI) focuses on both 'Practical' and 'Explain' tasks. Although 'Explain' tasks are essential in TBI, we argue that they are less effective than 'Practical' tasks, which are valued for their learning potential. Considering that 'Explain' tasks can be seen as less engaging and less relevant in practical settings, we argue that TBI should prioritize 'Practical' tasks. Ultimately, we advocate for a more efficient and effective Task-Based Instruction (TBI) that focuses on 'Practical' tasks.

We've developed a method for determining the density matrix of an quantum state without collapsing it, called shadow tomography. This approach only requires a specific type of measurement once per state component, as opposed to repeating the measurements for multiple realizations. Although it seems to be a hard problem to get an exact density matrix from these measurements, we found that it's relatively simple to estimate each state component with some level of uncertainty. By taking the average of multiple measurements, we can get closer to the actual value, despite not having exact data. We can utilize this average in a variety of mathematical algorithms that make use of multiple measurements, such as minimum relative entropy and maximum marginal probability, to estimate the density matrix. We found that one such algorithm, using the average data, is able to get surprisingly close to the actual density matrix even with a small number of measurements, as long as the state isn't too mixed. We also found that it's possible to get this average data using just one specific type of measurement, rather than requiring a bunch of different measurements, as long as the state has some special properties. By utilizing this average data in a mathematical algorithm, we can get the density matrix for states that have these special properties.

In this paper, we establish min-max-max inequalities for the inradius and circumradius of convex polygons with a given perimeter, along with maximum and minimum values of their products, with respect to various area measures based on harmonic and geometric means. These area formulas are previously published by the current paper's author, and this study utilizes them to establish these inequalities, and also determines the extreme polygon configurations that achieve these extreme values.

This study introduces an innovative trajectory design approach for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) by leveraging their capacity for mobile base station deployment. The problem is cast as an optimized route planning issue to allow the UAV to provide the greatest value to users by delivering critical services (e.g., user demand). By converting the challenge into a variant of the orienteering problem, combined with an information theoretic technique, the proposed approach achieves a more efficient route planning solution. The solution incorporates two algorithms: a binary decision heuristic for solving an integer optimization problem and a greedy algorithm for quick deployment. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that this solution delivers average performance within 300% to 400% of that achieved by the best existing approach.

Recent studies have revealed complex phenomena in bilayer graphene, which exhibits characteristics of both Dirac and Klein-Gordon equations depending on the layer alignment. At low temperatures, the material displays nematic properties on a specific angular fundamental space, resulting from interlayer symmetry breaking. This breaking gives rise to a specific rotation symmetry within the Pmmn symmetry group. However, theories suggest the material should not exhibit this breaking, instead preserving the rotation symmetry. Utilizing topological angle and strain deformations, we simulate nematic states in the material. Our findings indicate the material's angular symmetry can be either preserved or broken, contingent upon the strain direction and quality of the nematic state. Additionally, the symmetry of the Dirac points and associated zero modes is discussed.

Investigations into magnetic and electric properties of endofullerenes on an Cu(111) substrate have been conducted using Scanning Tunneling Microscopy and Spectroscopy, as well as density functional theory at zero temperature and without influence from the substrate. The primary focus of these experiments has been on N@C80, C80 on threefold hollow sites, and C80 on fourfold hollow sites. The results show that endofullerenes exhibit distinct conformational differences when adsorbed on a substrate, leading to varying magnetic and electric properties, and possibly altering kinetic properties. The experimental findings have been supported by calculated total and spin-polarized density of states, as well as charge differences and spin densities of atoms. The properties of endofullerenes have been contrasted with those of a flat, monolayer graphite film.

The rapid expansion of the Internet of Things (IoT) has led to security and privacy issues being brought to the forefront. With data being shared between devices in an highly interconnected network, there is a heightened concern about potential threats. A cutting-edge solution to address these concerns is being developed through Federated Machine Learning (FML), which allows for model training without compromising individual data privacy. By leveraging MLSim, a multiparty simulation framework for JVMs, we have created a pioneering approach to training a multi-party model on IoT data without exchanging data. Our innovation uses JVMs on distinct devices, which communicate through MLSim, enabling a secure and private environment for model training. Through FML and MLSim, any IoT device can be transformed into a secure data generator, allowing for a secure and private environment for model training. Our method has been successfully tested on devices such as Android smartphones, Raspberry Pis, Android TVs, and the training process took place on an existing Nuxalk dataset using an MLSim implementation on a multi-node Apache Flink cluster.

To efficiently perform sensitive low-fidelity Ramsey measurements, we incorporate Bayesian experiment design, which two alternative techniques - adaptive heuristic design and random design - are also employed for comparison. Our findings indicate that the Bayesian approach achieves the smallest measurement uncertainty while the heuristic method is suitable for situations involving incomplete or incomplete knowledge of relevant factors. Notably, the Bayesian and heuristic designs yield comparable results when all key factors are accounted for, suggesting the Bayesian protocol could be replaced by its heuristic counterpart in such cases. Although the Bayesian protocol offers optimal performance, the heuristic protocol offers the benefit of being easily executed without requiring detailed analysis or understanding of the underlying system, making it a more accessible option for researchers familiar only with the system's inputs and outputs.

The application of Gromov centrality in characterizing various network types has been explored. This method distingu/ is distinguished by its capacity to detect Gromov vector-dependent irregularities within the betweenness centrality of nodes in different network models. In real-world networks, Gromov centrality proves more sensitive than the conventional Gromov vector-dependent anomaly detected with the Mahalanobis distance. This is seen in inanimate and Facebook networks where the Gromov centrality reveals a finer distinction between different node types. Additionally, the Gromov centrality helps to separate nodes more effectively across different network types.

According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, connected objects slowly move away from one another over time due to their gravitational linkages.  This theory appears to align with observations indicating an increasing mean Earth-Sun distance over time.  However, when combined with the mean Earth-Sun mass and mean orbital radius, Newton's law yields a value for the mean gravitational force acting upon the Earth as it orbits the Sun that is less than the mean centripetal force required for its observed orbit, a discrepancy of approximately 3.5 times 10 to the power of 16 joules per meter.  This minor mismatch is resolvable using the mean energy transfer theory described in the author's work, a framework founded upon the premise that the Earth's and Sun's gravitational linkages are composed of two separate components, one that adheres to general relativity and another that may deviate from it.  This second element, based on the idea of the Sun being at the center of an expanding universe, is thought to be responsible for the minor discrepancy.

We investigate complex matrices and their matrix polynomial bundles by analyzing their spectral properties. Utilizing Groebner theory, we demonstrate that certain open and closed bundles share similar spectral characteristics. Building on these findings, we establish a relationship between the resolvent problem's solvability and the bundle's open or closed nature. As a result, we derive both necessary and sufficient conditions for solvability, depending on the bundle's properties. Additionally, we establish a link between the matrix's eigenvalue distribution and the bundle's open or closed properties, specifically spectral set estimates.

The development of non-geometric phase theory in string theory has significantly advanced our understanding, particularly in the context of B-folds in F-theory and generalised Hermitian and non-Hermitian matrices. Our work exhibits the connection between the concept of classical T-duality in non-geometric string theory and the properties of continuous-trace algebras. This connection is rooted in the fact that non-geometric string theory's phase space corresponds to the cone of continuous-trace group algebras. Within the scope of this theory, Flory duality is observed to encompass a form of classical T-duality. Our analysis also explores the relationship between the commutative case of continuous-trace algebras, generalised Hermitian matrices, and non-geometric string theory's phase space. Ultimately, we demonstrate that non-geometric T-duality is implemented through transformations of generalized Hermitian matrices, thereby generalizing flux quads and the non-geometric B^2-instanton. Furthermore, we dissect the instantonic properties of the non-geometric phase in F-theory by utilising its underlying non-Abelian 5-brane geometry, specifically in the context of the deranged and inverted deranged B-folds. Additionally, we have found that T-duals of deranged and inverted deranged B-folds exhibit the characteristics of forming self-dual and anti-self-dual algebras, thereby providing a physical explanation

In recent years, researchers have given special consideration to the computational demands of discrete Baker's approaches in algorithmic motion planning within graph structures. Our contributions comprise the development of faster, more efficient solutions to several motion planning related problems for graphs lacking minor faults, facilitated through an innovative and novel embedding technique that reduces the time required to solve these problems by a significant margin. Specifically, this advancement allows for a dramatic 74-fold improvement over prior works in relation to the computational resources needed to solve these problems in graph structures, under comparable computational complexity limits. To achieve this breakthrough, we employ an innovative method for embedding long paths within carefully designed restricted graph patterns in a manner that minimizes distortion, resulting in a more efficient and time-conscious embedding approach that prioritizes computational feasibility and speed. Our solution to this problem involves addressing a series of challenging problems, including the creation of an efficient and novel sparsification tool for computing minimal spanning trees within specific graph patterns lacking minor faults, as well as an innovative and precise quantification of the distortion introduced by this new sparsification tool, in a manner that remains independent of any arbitrary parameters such as the vertex count, exhibiting a significant and remarkable improvement over prior sparsification tools by at least a factor of  O~{o}(1)  in relation to previous work and features a universally applicable and precise quantification that is independent of parameters such as vertex count and extends beyond just sparsification tools to general metric cut problems within specific graph patterns, as well as

In this study, we examine the time-periodic parabolic equation with nonlinearities that have supercritical growth in any dimension, using an unconventional approach by considering an ensemble of solutions generated from diverse initial conditions. By defining this ensemble and deriving its evolution based on these initial conditions and a given periodic equation, we are able to study its long-term behavior and prove the existence of periodic solutions that arise from this ensemble. Crucial to our findings is the impact of the prevalence of initial conditions, which determines the convergence of the ensemble to periodic solutions. Interestingly, even a small fraction of initial conditions contributing to the convergence can imply the existence of periodic solutions, even when none exists for a single solution. Additionally, we have established a maximum and minimum bound on the prevalence required for the existence of periodic solutions.

A key challenge in quantum computing is optimizing the performance of near-term devices.  This challenge can be addressed through the study of algorithms that run on these devices.  In this paper, a variational quantum eigensolver based on quantum neural networks called Quantum Echo-Based ADAPT VQE (QEB-ADAPT-VQE) is proposed.  This protocol utilizes a quantum echo-based strategy to determine the eigenstates of a given Hamiltonian with fewer iterations than previous ADAPT-VQE algorithms, utilizing fermionic, qubit, and Quantum Echo-Based formulations.  By utilizing fermionic circuit analogues in a qubit model, QEB-ADAPT-VQE can efficiently converge to its target eigenstates, utilizing a small number of quantum circuits.  As a result, QEB-ADAPT-VQE can efficiently run on near-term devices, with a numerical demonstration that it outperforms the fermionic- and qubit-ADAPT-VQE algorithms in convergence speed and efficiency on various molecular systems, with a notable improvement of 5-60 times in efficiency.  These results indicate that QEB-ADAPT-VQE offers a valuable approach for efficiently running quantum computing algorithms on near-term devices.  This protocol has been uploaded to the Quantum Circuit Catalogue at [www.qccatalog.com](http://www.qccatalog.com), with the hope that it can contribute to the development of near-term quantum computing algorithms.

A novel approach, the Deep Generative Decoder (DGD), was previously developed as a deep Bayesian variational inference method to implicitly define a manifold in a high-dimensional representation space. While initially used to identify the underlying structure of a single distribution, we modified the DGD to accommodate multiple class distributions. By adding a label input into the inference network, the DGD is forced to centre the representations of each class within separate areas of the representation space. This updated model is able to produce an implicit, manifold-based model for multiple distributions, achieving state-of-the-art results in various classification tasks. We applied the DGD to fall prevention from drop height using a large dataset of 118,418 sequences, and the DGD achieved state-of-the-art accuracy in three challenging motion prediction tasks. Our work also includes the integration of uncertainty quantification into the DGD to analyze the level of uncertainty within the acquired data, identify potential biases, and pinpoint key features that distinguish between classes.

We examine how adding a nearly weightless $m^2\phi^2$ Higgs doublet to the well-established $\Lambda$CDM+HR model addresses two longstanding cosmological tensions, namely the Hubble and $S_8$ tensions. By considering this new variable mass Higgs model, we simulate different cosmological scenarios using MontePython with three distinct prior settings for the scalar potential: flat, logarithmic, and non-flat. In each case, our simulation indicates that incorporating a near-minimalism scenario where the Higgs doublet's mass is very low can effectively alleviate the Hubble tension, with this near-minimalist scenario almost indistinguishable from the original $\Lambda$CDM+HR model in terms of theoretical predictions. Notably, our analysis shows that although the phase transition temperature is very low in this near-minimalist scenario, it does not pose any challenge to the scenario. We find that by increasing the dark radiation energy density to a very low level or by introducing a very stiff component with a negative equation of state, we can further reduce the Hubble and $S_8$ tensions, with the improved scenario dubbed as KNM2 model successfully reconciling these two tensions, as compared to the original $\Lambda$CDM+HR model which failed to reconcile them.

Our observations of the comet C/2015 ER61, specifically from data collected on April 7-8 when it was at a distance of approximately 1.8 astronomical units from Earth, provide insight into the behavior of volatile species during the comet's dynamic interaction with its solar environment. We utilized the ALMA millimeter continuum and spectral survey, analyzing 15 distinct molecules and 21 related isotopic variants. Our observations revealed a diverse range of gas release patterns, particularly that HCN outgassed more intensely as the comet approached the closer approach to the Sun, whereas other species such as CS, H$_2$CO, HNC, and CH$_3$OH were released at a constant rate. This phenomenon is attributed to the potentiality of HCN to form complexes with water, allowing it to maintain gas phase presence more effectively than other species, which could explain its distinctive outgassing pattern. Conversely, the outgassing patterns of H$_2$O are consistent with either radial-turbulent flow or water freezing, and the gas phase chemistry modeling of CS, H$_2$CO, HNC, and CH$_3$OH, despite yielding numerous agreements, also highlights the need for additional information regarding non-destructive loss processes, particularly photo-dissociation, photo-destruction, and chemical reactions, to fully understand volatile species release. Notably, the comet's deuterium enrichment ratio, which was found to be relatively low, is consistent with previous measurements

In a recent study, an unsupervised speech synthesis system was developed that
learns to mimic human speech patterns from a large dataset of spoken language
without needing a labeled training set. The system, which is based on sequence-to-
sequence convolutional neural networks, was compared to a supervised speech synthesis
system in terms of its ability to produce natural and easily understandable speech.
Using a range of evaluation metrics, the researchers found that the unsupervised system
clearly outperformed the supervised system, which struggled to produce speech with
the same level of clarity and overall sound quality. Additionally, the researchers
conducted a listening test involving human evaluators and found that people preferred
the speech produced by the unsupervised system, which sounded more like human speech
and had a more consistent tone and rhythm.

We're studying the interacting Tsallis-Hagedorn holographic dark energy model, which manages the universe's energy balance with interacting dark energy and matter. This model incorporates a single interacting coupling parameter, $\eta$, in addition to two essential constants, $c$ and $T_0$. Our focus is on the Tsallis $f$-mode distribution function, which is influenced by the coupling parameter $\eta$ but not by $c$ and $T_0$. These constants are, however, significant in the Tsallis $f$-mode distribution function. Moreover, the interaction coupling parameter $\eta$ can be interpreted as a constant $c$ value, indicating a specific thermodynamic equilibrium state with the Tsallis distribution function's single exponential behavior. This means that the coupling parameter $\eta$ not only governs the interacting dark energy and matter balance but also serves as a scale or reference parameter, setting the scale of Tsallis distribution function exponent $\delta$. This scale refers to the degree of non-additivity of Tsallis entropy.

A newly introduced Investment Ratio (IR) metric evaluates and compares solution approaches for optimization problems by considering the relative costs and benefits after conversion into feasible solutions. This is exemplified by promoting the Truncated Path Downhill algorithm, which effectively optimizes, by demonstrating its ability to obtain solutions with a higher Investment Ratio compared to other methods like Particle Swarm Optimization and Gravitational Search Algorithm.

In the framework of synthetic differential geometry, we've developed the notion of an $n$-jet source, which is an object with an attached $n$-jet simple path groupoid, consisting of objects with infinitely divisible $n$-jet components. These jet simple path groupoids can be seen as an extension of source path groupoids and source simply connected groupoids. By establishing a relationship between these jet simple path groupoids and free differential algebras over a commutative ring, we've effectively generalized classical $n$-jet notions to this synthetic differential setting.

The Dynaswap project is a multi-disciplinary effort that develops secure, collaborative software using cutting-edge technologies such as Virtual Machines, Provenance-based Reconciliation, and Zero-Knowledge Proofs. Our objective is to create a virtual object management system that allows multiple parties to share and track modifications to files and graphs. This paper outlines the project's framework, detailing the integration of cutting-edge technologies like VMs, VOPs, and Provenance-based Reconciliation. Additionally, we present the Dynaswap architecture and its key components, including the Dynaswap Virtual Machine, Virtual Object Manager, and Swap Tree. Furthermore, we introduce the Dynaswap workflow and its key functionalities like virtual object creation, sharing, and reconciliation, highlighting the features and benefits of our approach. Finally, we highlight potential research avenues related to access control, componentisation, and reconciliation, and outline how Dynaswap can be utilized in a variety of application scenarios, such as digital asset management, collaborative software, and blockchain-based block storage. Additionally, we include two case studies that demonstrate the integration of Dynaswap with existing blockchain-based systems, using Ethereum and Hyperledger Bitalbec as reference implementations.

Recent advancements in Contrastive Pre-training (CPT) have revolutionized the capture of semantic rich information from large-scale datasets. Nevertheless, the task of Aspect-based Sentiment Analysis (ABSA) still poses challenges, particularly in accurately identifying the sentiment orientation. To tackle this issue, this paper presents a novel approach that incorporates a Supervised CPT to distill robust sentiment orientations from product reviews. Notably, our approach also explores multiple techniques to refine the sentiment orientation representation. Empirical evidence and analysis confirm that our proposed method surpasses the performance of existing non-supervised CPT approaches. Additionally, our experiment demonstrates that a lower CPT temperature (soft clustering) yields more precise results compared to higher temperatures (coarse clustering).

Individuals taking gastric acid suppressors are at a greater risk of contracting listeriosis, a disease caused by the bacterium \textit{Listeria monocytogenes}, which targets individuals with reduced immune function. Although the established two-strain competitive interaction model has been shown to significantly delay the onset of listeriosis, making it less likely to occur even with the same initial bacterial counts, our research indicates that this delay is attributable to decreased bacterial interaction rather than altered host response time. Consequently, based on these findings, at least three factors are expected to contribute to the decreased likelihood of listeriosis: increased bacterial cooperation, elevated bacterial growth rates, and reduced host immune response. Furthermore, when initial bacterial counts favor \textit{Listeria monocytogenes}, the likelihood of listeriosis increases, while reduced immunocompetency has a diminished impact on its onset, but substantially diminishes the likelihood of survival. These insights, combined with the observation that the model predicts listeriosis is less likely to occur when initiated after symptoms emerge, underscore the significance of early bacterial co-cultivation in listeriosis development.

This study explores the impact of transceiver hardware impairments and energy harvesting in reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RISs) on secret communication in multiuser systems. Analyzing both general and special cases of RIS phase control, we derive a theoretical model for signal-to-interference-plus-noise power at each user, and subsequently, the overall sum through a general approach and optimal solution. We find that in most general cases, determining the optimal user power and RIS phase elements is computationally demanding and does not provide insight into the impact of hardware impairments. To address this limitation, we investigate a special case of RIS phase control and develop a theoretical model for the secret rate, and determine the optimal user power and RIS phase elements. We find that in this case, RIS phase control is not significantly affected by hardware impairments. Furthermore, we investigate energy harvesting in RISs and multiuser systems with a single energy harvester, and derive a theoretical model for the secrecy rate, and determine the optimal power allocation and energy harvesting efficiency. Notably, we find that in this case, RIS phase control does not affect the overall system performance. We confirm the theoretical results through both analytical and simulation methods.

Sequential self-supervised learning approaches can optimize predictive models by iteratively correcting past errors, a process reminiscent of hindsight summarization that could enhance learning outcomes.
