Conjointly working across clinical and data science sectors, a comprehensive toolkit called highdicom has been developed to enhance the interoperability of MRI, CT, and pathology data, including image analysis output. This toolchain facilitates seamless data exchange between hospitals and research institutions, as well as between diverse software applications, thereby empowering users to deploy innovative data science protocols while preserving their data's integrity. Highdicom effectively addresses the constraints imposed by legacy healthcare systems, harmonizing output formats and accounting for unique requirements of each domain. A unified programming interface, grounded in Python, promotes the use of open-source libraries, including
adicoms3, Nifti-IO, and Horus. By standardizing image and
parcellation data, highdicom promotes format consistency and
facilitates data ingestion into cloud-based storage systems and
visualization platforms.

Although our description of the horizon includes diffeomorphism effects, 
we prove that when identifying the horizon in its most simplified form, 
these effects are cancelled out and the structure of the horizon remains 
unchanged under transformations, provided the transformation is a general 
relativity mapping. In the investigation of the horizon, 
these effects prove to be insignificant and the simplified model of the 
horizon is adequate. Since the expression for the entropy in terms of the 
surface area depends only on the exterior metric, which remains unchanged 
under diffeomorphisms, no new constraints are imposed on the entropy by 
diffeomorphism invariance. In addition, the identity relating the metric and 
the Chern-Simons form, which is used in the calculation of the entropy, 
depends only on the exterior, thus also making the calculation independent 
of the interior metric, and therefore the interior metric can be arbitrary.

Our findings indicate that the most critical characteristics for solving the DNA classification task are not all biological in nature. The most relevant features include those from 2nd order DNA (triplets) and 4th order DNA (quadruplets) signals, which are also statistically significant and provide understandable predictions. These results align with previous studies, suggesting that the underlying biological processes dictate feature importance. Furthermore, the key features' effects are consistent at the DNA, protein, and disease levels, offering analogous interpretations. Lastly, the model's transferability to related genetic alteration data highlights the relevance of our findings to translational medicine.

This article explores the relationship between the breakdown of sum rules in spectral weight and the properties of insulating phases within strongly correlated systems that undergo a metal-insulator transition. We concentrate on the specific case of the Hubbard model on a square lattice, analyzing numerical results where the model is subjected to unidirectional spatial confinement. In this confined Hubbard model, the breakdown of sum rules is more pronounced in the confined direction, yet survives certain choices of parameters, even in the insulating phase of small gap size. Comparing these findings with lessons learned from unidirectional confinement is crucial in understanding the origin and magnitude of spectral weight discrepancies. Furthermore, the model with spatial confinement offers a unique platform to investigate the role of charge fluctuations in various phases of the Hubbard model, especially the correlated insulating phase, which can accommodate fluxes of symmetry-protected topological order. As a consequence, the nature of the Fermi gaps in this insulating phase is an exception to the rule that relates gap size to the spectral weight. Moreover, the Hubbard model with spatial confinement provides a setting to simulate an electron-interaction-driven metal-insulator transition from a known topological insulating phase, whose surface states are exposed to the influence of a confining potential, serving as a model for the experimental exploration of topological phases and phase transitions.

A new class of symplectic integrators on coadjoint orbits is developed by adapting existing techniques from unitary dynamics and Poisson-algebra theory. These collective integrators consistently preserve coadjoint orbits, a critical property also inherent in Lie-Poisson equations, as well as their corresponding energy and angular momentum characteristics. Notably, our approach allows for the construction of integrators tailored to any Lie algebra, thereby accommodating diverse applications such as the Euclidean and pseudo-Euclidean spaces commonly used in both theoretical and experimental physics. By implementing these integrators in the study of the planar Euler-Lagrange system and the generalised Kepler problem, we observe the preservation of coadjoint orbits, Casimirs, and an extended phase space's Hamiltonian, all in perfect harmony with an additional discrete symmetry. These results not only advance the understanding of dynamical behaviour on coadjoint orbits but also inspire the development of new integrators for studying interacting particles subject to boundaries or external forces.

Despite significant progress in microlensing detection, currently available software has limitations in identifying planets with specific mass ratios when their existence is not predetermined. To address these gaps, researchers are developing new software to analyze microlensing, including a novel software for independent discovery of planets using existing data. The tool is built on established software for microlensing analysis, including a specific algorithm for identifying planets in 2L5P models. To improve planet detection, this software can now also use an unsupervised machine learning technique called Gaussian Process Empirical Bayes (GPEB) in combination with a novel, model-independent algorithm using a GPEB-2L4P model. The discovered planets include a number of exoplanets with distinct characteristics such as a Venus-like exoplanet in OGLE-2018-BLG-1204, which has a very low mass ratio, a M dwarf in OGLE-2018-BLG-1134, which has a distinct mass ratio, and several other planets in various observed microlensing events. The developed software using GPEB-2L4P model outperformed the traditional method based on 2L5P models by identifying more planets with specific mass ratios when their existence is not known in advance.

We create an explicit resolution approach for implicit time discretizations
in conservation laws with a unique flux gradient computation path.
Traditionally, solving implicit time discretizations requires iterative
solutions, but our method uses only one iteration while allowing direct
access to the solution at the first time step with its desired accuracy.
This new approach is compared in numerical tests to other standard solving
methods and shows comparable or improved accuracy while being more
efficient by reducing the number of iterative steps needed.

The preemption of non-performing loans is a priority for policies in numerous Asian nations. This study examines the application of machine learning and deep learning models for predicting NPLs in an Asian bank, using a multivariate time series dataset. We compared the performance of several models, including a basic logistic model and enhanced options like logistic models coupled with wavelet transforms, various types of neural networks, and a deep learning model integrating convolutional and recurrent layers. According to our results, the deep autoencoder model achieved the highest accuracy and area under the ROC curve, followed by the logistic model enhanced with wavelet transforms. Based on these findings, we suggest implementing the deep autoencoder model for forecasting NPLs, and using models combining wavelet transforms and deep learning for creating NPL prediction algorithms in parallel. This study's methods and data can be applied to forecasting NPLs in other institutions and sectors.

We have identified a connection between the $q$-analogue of chromatic symmetric functions and certain $q$-analogues of classical symmetric functions such as the $q$-hit numbers and the elementary symmetric functions. This relationship inspired the discovery of a $q$-analogue of the Stanley--Givental inversion formula, leading to the derivation of new results regarding $q$-analogues of classical poset invariants. Specifically, we have developed formulas for the $q$-version of the Foulkes' conjecture and for $q$-analogues of the Nekrasov--Shatashvili $e$-function. Our approach utilizes flag $q$-analogues of combinatorial objects such as $q$-analogues of Dyck paths, Kreweras' animals, and non-attacking permutations, as well as recent results regarding the equivalence of the $q$-analogue of chromatic symmetric functions to $q$-hit numbers. Moreover, we have devised a method for proving $q$-analogues of poset invariants by providing a $q$-version of the $P$-partitions bijection.

This research introduces Landmark Gabor Filters (LGFs) as an alternative to traditional Gabor Filters (GFs), aiming to improve robustness of image representations against variations in object orientation. LGFs are a type of complex-valued filter that extracts unique patterns from an image, similar to GFs. However, LGFs utilize a more adaptable and robust landmark-based alignment mechanism instead of a precise and precise alignment mechanism, allowing the filters to be evenly distributed across all possible orientations. As a result, LGFs provide more effective image representations and better tolerance to orientation changes. Additionally, our research provides an analysis of the impact of training data quality and quantity on the robustness of image representations and introduces a new technique for enhancing the uniqueness of landmark-based patterns.

Building on previous findings in [AD22], we establish a relative fundamental lemma for group schemes over a Dedekind domain, with applications in computing and estimating orbital integrals as well as deriving explicit local functional equations for L-functions within this framework.

In the context of two-flavor QCD, we investigate how heavy quark masses influence the QCD coupling and precision calculations related to the pion's leptonic form factor and light quark masses in the high-energy regime where heavy quarks dominate. Utilizing hard thermal loop (HTL) renormalization group (RG) techniques incorporating heavy quark mass effects, we integrate these considerations into our analysis. By combining invariants representing novel dressing effects at high energy, we then evaluate their impact on various dispersion relations associated with the integrated and differential cross-sections of e+e- → hadrons, specifically those involving hadron masses, angular distributions, and the production of light particles. These investigations require precise control over finite mass effects, and our work demonstrates how heavy quark masses can modify lighter quark mass values and precision QCD coupling in a manner compatible with experimental data and predictions from perturbative calculations.

A graph is said to be correctly k-colored if the edges can be colored with k colors such that no consecutive edges in the vertices' sequence have the same color. The minimum number of colors required for correct edge-coloring of a graph G is denoted by γ(G). Research has shown that for a graph meeting a certain criterion (G's degree difference between the vertices being at least 1) also has the property of being correctly 2k+1 edge-colored, with evidence provided through a C4-free graph and n=13 or more, with n being the number of vertices in the graph.

The nature of the elements in weighted Bergman spaces on the unit disk can be defined by two key factors - the integral of the absolute value of the functions over the disk and the rate at which they increase in magnitude towards the boundary. By applying the Carleson-Nyström theorem, which provides a practical way to determine if a given set of functions constitutes a Riemann surface over the unit disk, specific criteria have been established for the necessary and sufficient conditions for normality of Gaussian processes in the context of weighted Bergman spaces. Building upon these findings, additional criteria have been derived for normality of Gaussian processes in other types of function spaces on the unit disk and have been generalized to $p$-Grammelian spaces.

Initially response-theoretic incremental structural learning models were developed to mimic humans' incremental learning abilities. These models are capable of adapting to new data while retaining previously learned information, similar to how humans process new information in relation to existing knowledge. This research aims to apply initially response-theoretic incremental structural learning models to the diagnosis of critical conditions such as COVID-19, pneumonia, and influenza by analyzing chest X-ray images. Additionally, the study investigates whether incorporating meta-data would enhance the models' performance. Our research indicates that initially response-theoretic incremental structural learning models are superior to other current AI models diagnosing COVID-19 and influenza, while performing similarly to the best models in diagnosing pneumonia. Furthermore, the utilization of meta-data significantly improves the sensitivity and accuracy of the models across all three conditions.

This research focuses on the design and modeling of large-scale satellite formations, with a primary goal of reducing the footprint of their orbital tracks to minimize the risk of collisions with critical infrastructure. The study introduces a novel, underexplored area of investigation, namely using non-identical satellites in a formation to achieve this goal, with the aim of making this approach more feasible in low-earth orbit (LEO) where numerous satellite constellations are being deployed in the form of mega-constellations, grid formations, and other configurations. The work outlines two primary methods - the "spread" method utilizing non-identical satellites and its standard counterpart using identical satellites, along with an idealized "cluster" method for comparison, before analyzing their effectiveness in terms of reducing the formation's overall footprint, with the "spread" method demonstrating superiority in this aspect. Furthermore, the study defines and utilizes minimum space occupancy (MiSO) orbits to quantify the reduced formation size achieved through optimized placement, with the "spread" method again demonstrating significant size reduction potential across a range of LEO altitudes for formations of up to 100 satellites or more. The findings of this research are highly applicable in the design and scaling of satellite mega-constations for both military and commercial use, with the "spread" method providing a practical solution for reducing the visibility and potential for interference of such formations over time.

In mesh generation, uniformly arranged quadrilaterals are often desired for simplicity. Unfortunately, given a triangulated surface, finding an optimal linear arrangement of quadrilaterals is a challenging problem with no known solution. However, in this study, we propose a partial solution by revising a well-established method of quadrilateral mesh generation with T-mesh splitting. The key innovation is that linearly connected quadrilaterals can capture sharp features, effectively allowing for the simplification of a given linear quad layout. Furthermore, our method enables the automatic division of surfaces with arbitrary geometry and provides a straightforward way to preserve specified boundary conditions. The proposed algorithm is illustrated with several examples, highlighting its versatility and efficiency.

When evaluating the correlation between two variables, p-values are frequently used 
in order to determine the strength of their association. Many statistical methods, such as regression and classification, do this by conducting tests that are sensitive to the variables' associations. In instances where the dataset's true distribution isn't well-defined or isn't normal, researchers often resort to approximating p-values using correlation coefficients' asymptotic formulas, assuming a normal distribution. However, we propose a different approach: using permutation tests in specific cases where the dataset's joint distribution is defined by non-Gaussian functions. By doing so, we're able to obtain more accurate p-values than those obtained from correlation coefficients' formulas, particularly when evaluating the correlations in samples that are drawn from mixed Gaussian distributions with distinct means and standard deviations.

A approach inspired by 't Hooft's concept of the $C$-theorem is proposed, which uses the quantum $S$-matrix to analyze the properties of black holes. This method is particularly suited to investigate theoretical models of gravity that describe black holes in a quantum context. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we applied this approach to a black hole model derived using the Hartle-Hawking path integral, which provides a mathematical representation of (anti)-de Sitter space with a mass gap. In this model, a specific observable, analogous to the $C$-function, can be calculated using the $S$-matrix, which is a fundamental concept in quantum field theory that describes scattering processes. When applied to a massless scalar field in an expanding (anti)-de Sitter universe with a mass gap, the resulting $S$-matrix reveals a function, denoted as $\mathcal{S}$, whose behavior is well-defined across all possible values of the curvature radius $a$. This is due to a specific asymptotic limit in the $\mathcal{S}$ function, which is unaltered when either the curvature radius or the mass gap are infinitely large. Consequently, a "quantum $S$-matrix" inequality of the form $|\mathcal{S}(a_+,c)| \leq |\mathcal{S}(a_-,c)|$ is established, which holds for any value of the mass gap $c = \frac

We've demonstrated, using the theory of Navier-Stokes dynamics near unstable equilibria in a two-dimensional plane, that using localized feedback controls can significantly reduce the stabilization time in comparison to controls with global reach. This breakthrough was achieved through the application of the Viscous Potentials Method and the construction of stream-function feedback controls, whose corresponding velocity fields are localized and classical in nature. The effects of quantum noise on stabilization are also explored, resulting in the discovery of an additional, constant factor affecting the required stabilization time. The insights gained from our research have implications for understanding experimental findings where stabilization times with localized feedback are significantly reduced compared to those with global feedback.

The LitMind Dictionary is an open-source, web-based mind mapping tool that displays mind maps in a visual format and provides definitions from a built-in dictionary.  Initially created in MindManager, the dictionary has been converted to various formats such as JSON and CSV, allowing for its integration with different programming languages.  Originally supported languages including English, French, Spanish, German and Italian, the dictionary has been updated to also support Portuguese and Russian.  A JSON plugin enables the generation of JSON files, while a CSV plugin allows for the creation of CSV files, both of which can be imported into external applications such as Excel.  Additionally, the file format of the exported files can be specified, including those compatible with languages like JavaScript and XML.  A user can choose from file types such as JSON, CSV, or XML, with the option to also map the JSON structure for a single entry.  With the LitMind Dictionary's plug-ins, the user can control the file type and format, and even specify a language other than the default language of the mind map.

A growing number of recommender systems are being designed with explainability in mind, as researchers and practitioners believe that providing explicit explanations will enhance user understanding, thereby leading to improved outcomes. Since many recommender systems are not fully transparent due to their complex black-box nature, explanations are typically generated post-hoc from available model outputs. However, we suggest that even if a recommender system is considered explainable, its recommendations may still be unreliable due to potential inconsistencies between its predictions and actual user preferences. This phenomenon can be addressed by incorporating an uncertainty quantification component that adjusts recommendations based on an external survey of user preferences. Two resampling techniques, parametric bootstrapping and non-parametric sampling, are proposed to incorporate external preferences into the recommendation process. Experimental results using real-world data indicate that incorporating uncertainty quantification results in more robust recommendations, as well as better alignment between recommendations and actual user preferences. Notably, our approach does not necessitate any direct interaction with users, as recommendations and their confidence levels are automatically generated based on model outputs and the external preference survey data. This methodology enables researchers and practitioners to improve the reliability of recommender systems without requiring further user input.

A novel heterostructure has been developed on a SnTe substrate with an In$_{0.81}$Ga$_{0.19}$As capping layer, where the presence of indium was verified through x-ray fluorescence. Characterization via X-ray photoemission spectroscopy revealed that the SnTe surface features a strong oxidized layer, while the In$_{0.81}$Ga$_{0.19}$As capping layer contains no oxygen. Notably, the SnTe surface was originally at the surface Fermi level, but this was shifted deeper into the bulk by the presence of the In$_{0.81}$Ga$_{0.19}$As capping layer. Moreover, photoemission measurements detected a strong Sn 4d signal from the In$_{0.81}$Ga$_{0.19}$As interface, indicating that Sn atoms penetrate this layer during molecular beam epitaxy growth and, upon heating, In$_{0.81}$Ga$_{0.19}$As reconstructs to allow Sn to move towards the substrate.

This research focuses on the challenge of developing distribution-free and adaptively learning concepts when the teacher's advice relies on a radius-based metric. Annotators receive hidden information about each data sample, including its distance from the teacher's advice. A concept class is said to possess the 'influence radius' property, if performance does not degrade for all instances where the radius of the query stays within a certain bound, regardless of the data distribution. Throughfully adaptive inquiries, it is demonstrated that robust learning is possible under this radius-based feedback, with both non-Bayesian and Bayesian approaches having the same sample complexity. Additionally, it is shown that an information-theoretic limit exists, with no matter how the annotator generates the hidden information, the requirement becomes stringent as the radius approaches zero. A new non-Bayesian pseudo-dimension measure is introduced, with the identification of a minimally complex concept class that requires this measure to characterise the learning requirement. Furthermore, it is established that robust learning under distributional assumptions necessitates a lower number of data samples, with the identification of a bound for this requirement. A distribution-free learning lower bound is also established for well-separated concepts.

The FS-2 algorithm, introduced in \cite{pontier2022fast}, offers a substantial speed boost for computing optimal transport (OT) plans by leveraging a technique called relaxation. However, the original implementation of FS-2 is plagued by instability and statistical instability, which renders it unreliable in practice. In this study, we develop a conceptually similar yet stable and efficient method called RelaxOT and demonstrate its effectiveness with real-world data from the fields of computer vision and statistical physics.

Direct imaging techniques have made it possible to detect exoplanets close to their stars through infrared light. However, since exoplanets and their host stars have different temperatures, changes in the temperature of the star can affect the amount of atmospheric mass loss of the exoplanet. By observing AU Mic, a young star with active flares, researchers were able to detect how the flares of the star would impact the atmosphere of its exoplanet, which is named AU Mic b. The mass loss of the exoplanet was found to be 10 times higher when the star's temperature increased due to a flare. The flares of the star also caused a change in the exoplanet's 3.5 micron light, indicating a different atmospheric mass loss process at this wavelength. The increased mass loss of the exoplanet was found to be 10-100 times higher in the 3.5 micron light, which is likely due to the water content of the exoplanet's atmosphere decreasing.

Investigating particle scattering in a resistive medium with radiation, our research reveals an additional force affecting particles - radiation friction, which causes matter to warp around particles as they move. This effect leads to altered particle dynamics, particularly in strong fields, leading to changes in how particles cluster. Implications of our findings include potential impacts on cosmic rays, including the possibility of changing their flight paths, and a need for revised models of particle acceleration in such environments, which current theories may underestimate by a factor of two due to radiation effects alone.

The vast majority of pretreated imbalanced datasets in real-world applications are managed using techniques such as oversampling, undersampling, and hybrid approaches that prioritize diversity. However, these methods fall short in addressing the fundamental imbalance present in data, and furthermore, they lack a solid theoretical foundation. Contrasting conventional strategies, our approach develops enhanced pre-processing and learning algorithms by merging insights from statistics, information theory, and artificial intelligence, focusing specifically on majoritarian and minority classification. Our proposed frameworks utilize a set of adaptable threshold values, effectively fine-tuning the balance between accuracy and false positive/negative rates. Additionally, our analysis reveals that majoritarian classification under certain conditions can be a viable and useful pursuit in its own right, often benefiting from exclusive focus. As such, we're able to propose an alternative system of measures that better suits the intricate nature of imbalance, offering a more subtle and informative analysis of algorithm performance. Our experimental evaluations demonstrate the efficacy of our methods on a range of previously unaddressed imbalanced datasets in practice.

Twenty-five previously undiscovered Southern QSOs, detected through UV, VIS, IR, and submillimeter observations, were found in the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. The newly discovered QSOs include twenty lying beyond z=5 and five above U=18 including one extremely luminous QSO at z=7. The study utilized multi-color observations for absolute magnitude calculations and analyzed submillimeter data for two low-luminosity QSOs, also identifying potential host galaxies for two objects at z=4.7 and 5.2 using deep submillimeter images. The submillimeter flux of one extremely luminous QSO at z=7, however, could not be determined due to its limited observed submillimeter flux range. The study found that two newly discovered QSOs at z=4.8 and z=5.2 have submillimeter flux limited to 2.0 and 1.0 millijoules, respectively, and for the first time, for a QSO above U=18.

A quantum dot attached to a superconductor can serve as a highly sensitive device, capable of identifying and characterizing specific energy patterns within the superconductor through changes in hybridized states. Researchers have now proposed utilizing a quantum dot as a sensor to study the superconductor's energy patterns under varying widths, caused by the superconductor's energy gap and a nearby gate electric field. By analyzing the quantum dot's energy patterns, researchers found that certain energy patterns can be identified as belonging to the superconductor, even when the quantum dot's energy patterns are modified. Our study employs advanced analysis tools, including a transfer matrix and two analytical methods, to provide insight into the superconductor's width and energy patterns, offering a highly sensitive and quantitative means of studying complex materials such as disordered superconductors.

Our research focuses on the properties of shocks within two-dimensional, isentropic magnetohydrodynamics. By utilizing a contraction principle, it's determined that the two-dimensional isentropic magnetohydrodynamics shock is non-converging when there's no magnetic field. When there's a magnetic field, under specific conditions regarding the sign and strength, shocks will converge. These findings align with previous numerical simulations.

This research targets the challenging task of generating an endless perspective of a static scene from a single fixed camera, a viewpoint rotation that does not change over time. Three distinct techniques have been developed to create continuous, seamless video sequences capturing a scene from various rotating viewpoints. Two new methods, one employing 2D mesh transformation and the other as a fully 3D framework, guarantee an aesthetically pleasing, mathematically consistent perspective of the scene. Although these approaches are different in nature, they are both effective at generating realistic, infinitely looping video sequences. Additionally, this research demonstrates how these new 3D-based methods can be used to create new video clips even if the original images have been distorted or if there are holes in the image data, a technique known as warping. Several different methods have been utilized to create new, unrealized views of a scene, including a simplified 2D method and two more complex 3D-based techniques that rely on a fully 3D framework or Monte Carlo-based sampling. By using these new 3D-based techniques, it is possible to create new, unclosed image surfaces, a technique known as delving into a new, unclosed image volume, a technique known as volumetric rendering. Additionally, this research demonstrates how these new techniques can be used to create an infinite perspective of a human face, a technique known as face animation, and a related technique known as generating images from a single spherical image volume, a technique known as spherical volume

In the realm of model predictive real-time control, selecting an optimal solution typically involves a computationally demanding process. This paper introduces a novel strategy that utilizes the Koopman operator for dimension reduction, thereby capitalizing on its inherent properties to facilitate straightforward predictive control calculations. This Koopman-based approach to model predictive control is theoretically sound and has been experimentally validated in complex dynamic networks characterized by non-linear nodes and random delays. In practical terms, this method offers a significant computational advantage by offering a much smaller, yet efficient, reduction of system order. This in turn enables the calculation of optimal predictive control inputs in a much shorter time, specifically linear in the order of the system and the number of time steps. This time reduction can be observed in applications such as traffic systems, vehicle formations, wireless sensor networks, and others. Furthermore, this method has been further enhanced by implementing an online spectral decomposition technique in order to facilitate the determination of the optimal predictive control inputs in even complex large-scale networks characterized by spatially distributed randomness. This method of determining the optimal predictive control inputs in even time-varying and non-convex systems has been demonstrated in vehicle formations, wireless sensor networks, and intelligent traffic systems.

The instability of a liquid film on a fibre due to a slip condition at its base is studied, where the effect of this single point slip is compared to that of a small patch of slipped surface. It's found that the instability occurs more rapidly when the slip is confined to a small patch, but the shape of the droplet that forms critically depends on the size of the slipped area, with different shapes forming under different scenarios.

Derived novel Eulerian- Lagrangian mapping equations that differ from well-known Beltrami, Beltrami-Zel'dovich, and Aris equations. These new equations have the advantage of being free from artificial numerical dissipation and can maintain the original Lagrangian structure in Eulerian space. Furthermore, this work explores the potential impact on General Relativity when employing the new mapping equations, specifically in generating a correct Schwarzschild metric from a polynomial Lagrangian and accurately calculating a quadrupole mass parameter in adiabatic invariance.

The aim of this study was to assess the accuracy of using a robotic ultrasound to measure the angle of spinal processes in patients with scoliosis by comparing the results with the established ScolioGraphy method. To this end, the Oulu ScolioGraphy, a reliable and widely used technique for determining spinal curvature through ultrasound imaging, was employed as a reference standard to assess the angles of spinal processes in 20 patients with scoliosis. Meanwhile, the robotic ultrasound device was set to automatically adjust the transducer for optimal imaging. As scoliosis cases often display asymmetrical characteristics, the Oulu ScolioGraphy was applied using both left and right ultrasound images to calculate the angles of spinal processes from the images. These process angles were then evaluated at three levels (thoracic, lumbar, and sagittal) to yield total curvature angles at these sites. Two experienced radiologists independently analyzed the Oulu ScolioGraphy images to estimate curvature levels at the thoracic, lumbar, and sagittal sites, utilizing manual tracing and curvature measurement techniques. These estimates were then compared to the angles of spinal processes measured through the Oulu ScolioGraphy, yielding mean and standard deviations for the differences in estimates, denoted as delta bar and sigma. Delta bar represented the mean deviation of the robotic measurements from the Oulu ScolioGraphy measurements, indicating the systematic error, while sigma represented the random error. A statistically significant, moderate correlation was found

This study aims to integrate economic capital calculations with duration modeling, incorporating the model's predicted outcomes into risk-adjusted capital calculations and optimal portfolio selection. A primary contribution of this research lies in a novel duration modeling approach, which deviates from traditional methods by acknowledging that duration is a function of time and past outcomes. This is in contrast to conventional models, which typically operate under a no-arbitrage or Vasicek framework or simply predict future volatility. Furthermore, the proposed model is capable of handling non-conditional, conditional, and extreme value scenarios. The approach utilizes a dynamic factor model, specifically the ARFIMA model, to forecast durations. The finite sample properties and performance of the model are assessed through a portfolio selection experiment.

We're releasing a smaller, more balanced dataset for NLP research on hate
speech identification, drawn from Twitter. Our dataset is derived from 1,000
tweets, with an even split of hate speech and neutral content, and has been
labeled using a range of detailed categories. We conducted experiments using
sixteen NLP models, including various complex architectures, and found that
three specialized hate speech models - HL-T5, HL-BERT, and RNN-LSTM - outperformed
baseline models, achieving a high classification accuracy of 85.9% for the
task. Our dataset is designed to support further research in hate speech
identification, and is accessible at https://hate-speech-dataset.storage.googleapis.com/ hate_speech_identifier_v0.pdf.

Our analysis examines the MIMO framework's ability to isolate individual networks within the spectrum, specifically 3D MIMO, which fails to distinguish between overlapping networks in [1]. This failure stems from signaling characteristics that aren't naturally zero-mean. Our work introduces a new step for eliminating the crosstalk by subtracting the mean, thereby allowing the MIMO framework to accurately detect and separate 3D MIMO networks. Key benefits of our approach include enhanced MIMO network separation, increased dimensionality for signoring diversity, and heightened signal-to-noise ratio. This improved MIMO framework is applied to a real-world scenario - IoT device identification in wireless sensor networks. Furthermore, our methodology is made more efficient by utilizing a multi-instance learning strategy to reduce computational complexity and a "one-size-fits-all" approach to accommodate various IoT device configurations. Our findings show that even with highly overlapping signals, our method can accurately identify IoT devices, as illustrated through experiments using data collected under controlled environments. This study presents a groundbreaking approach for separating overlapping signals in real-world settings and has significant implications for IoT device identification.

Historical document analysis encompasses a range of complex tasks such as identifying and translating ancient texts, assessing their authenticity, and comprehension. While there are several notable datasets available for this field, locating relevant data for a specific time period, region, and research question remains a significant challenge. Our solution to this issue is the development of a dataset discovery tool, which allows users to specify a set of parameters defining the research scope and automatically identifies and suggests suitable datasets through the application of various search algorithms. By examining 107 English corpus-level datasets, our approach's effectiveness in suggesting at least one relevant dataset was evaluated based on the number of pages contained within each corpus. Our tool is now available online at the address historicaldatasetdiscovery.github.io.

This study proposes an innovative, model-free method for enhancing the accuracy of industrial robots tracking trajectories. The approach involves converting the measured joint angles into a reference torque signal, via a radial basis function neural network, and delivering it to the robot's joint actuators. We call this approach the Compliant Trajectory Following (CTF) method. To optimize the CTF approach, the reference torque signal is calculated using a predictive filter, based on past joint angle measurements. We conducted two experiments: one involving a simulated robot model and another with an actual ABB Yaskawa DA120.00 robot. The results indicate that the CTF method can reduce tracking errors by up to 300%, particularly in robot joints with significant elasticity, and also by about 70% in those with little or no elasticity.

Myocardial infarction patients who experience subsequent events within a 9 to 36 month timeframe tend to face a higher risk of dying. Research has focused largely on mycardial infarction risk recurrence and mortality in the immediate and short-term post-infarction period. Nevertheless, there is a need for investigations that examine the dynamics of heart disease risk over longer periods. This study employed techniques from myraid ensemble methods to create a predictive model for myocardial infarction recurrence, utilizing mycardial infarction patient data combined with socio-demographic and health data for London, England. The model developed in this study demonstrated mycardial infarction recurrence prediction capabilities over periods spanning 3-9 years, and even offered earlier warnings of impending events. The model also highlighted variations in the incidence of heart disease risk over time, influenced by socio-demographic factors such as ethnic group, sex, and age. This work presents mycardial infarction recurrence myraid as a highly effective tool for long-term heart disease risk monitoring and early myocardial infarction recurrence warning in patients.

We introduce an updated version of Becke's scheme for evaluating integrals involving the electronic continuum more efficiently. This improved method achieves convergence within a faster rate, specifically algebraic, which is comparable to that of an optimal rational function. It's particularly well-suited for calculations involving small error values, and we demonstrate its effectiveness by applying it to the Minkowski sum of an atomic basin over the entire space, as well as an atomic basin near a cleavage plane in a layered material. This method can be used directly in topological-atomic-models, and it also forms the basis for a new implementation of the decoupling approach by Ziegler and Granoulli\'er.

The Metric Dimension problem, which involves identifying a minimum number of nodes in a graph that allow for unique location determination using distance measurements, has been investigated further by focusing on specific graph parameters as constraints. It was found that when the problem is constrained by the number of vertices, clustering width, or the largest such value in a graph, it becomes computationally more manageable but still challenging to solve efficiently. However, when the problem is constrained by the graph's treewidth, it can be solved in a relatively short amount of time, utilizing a related theoretical framework. Building on this understanding, researchers were able to design an algorithm that utilizes a related theoretical framework to facilitate the solution of the Metric Dimension parameterized by treewidth, facilitating the solution of the Metric Dimension parameterized by treewidth.

In a directed complete partial order (dcpos), the Scott topology, lower, and upper topology are related but distinct concepts, with the latter being mutually exclusive. We introduce 'convex powerspaces' as a middle ground, characterized by being closed under convex subsets in a directed complete partial order. This characterizes them differently from powerspaces in discrete frames, as proven using the double powerframe object from the double stone representation of a distributive lattice. We also show that in a discrete space, convex powerspaces do not encompass the convex subsets. This characterization is further applied to the topology of a dcpo, converting the convex topology to an upper and a lower powerspace, but this is only possible if the dcpo is continuous, and the converse is true for a dcpo with a continuous order topology if the order is not the discrete topology, then the order is the convex topology's upper bounds space if and only if it is the discrete topology's lower bounds space, and the converse is true for a dcpo with a discrete topology if the dcpo is not continuous, and the dcpo is not the discrete topology if the dcpo is the convex topology's lower bounds space if and only if it is the discrete topology's upper bounds space.

In hothouse climates with low-latitude weather stations, water vapor continuum absorption significantly impacts radiative heating in the lower troposphere. This heating has far-reaching effects on hothouse climate patterns, influencing cloud coverage, precipitation patterns, and the quantity of saturated fuel available for atmospheric reactions. This research demonstrates that a weak heating from vapor absorption can create steady-state conditions in hothouse climates, characterized by increased precipitation and cloud coverage. By analyzing the equilibrium state, we find that a small amount of radiative heating necessary for steady atmospheric flow leads to water-rich fuel loads, resulting in more extensive precipitation and cloud coverage. This correlation is rooted in energy constraints within the climate system. This study showcases an often-overlooked aspect of vapor absorption in atmospheric chemistry and contributes to a deeper understanding of low-latitude climate patterns and behaviors.

This short report examines the theoretical framework of the higher-spin extension of Yang-Mills theory, featuring semisimple spectrum. The study focuses on three aspects: the deformation of the free action which includes an infinite number of higher-spin components, the connection to twisted self-dual systems, and the admixture with a Chern-Simons term, relevant in three-dimensional spacetime.

Deep learning networks have successfully resolved various classification challenges but are vulnerable to errors caused by large amounts of noisy data. To counter this issue, statistical analysis and data verification methods are combined to develop an enhanced network, specifically the Bayesian statistics guided label refurbishment mechanism (BLRM). This innovative approach integrates Bayesian statistics into a deep learning network to create an efficient data refinement system, which can be incorporated into a deep neural network to correct label errors and refine labels effectively. BLRM is designed to utilize training data with a low degree of label noise and to utilize both training and testing data with a high degree of label noise. To facilitate the Bayesian inference of label noise, BLRM utilizes a local neighborhood of each sample and a label loss function based on the maximum likelihood estimate of the joint probability distribution of labels and data. Utilizing the approximate Bayesian inference methods, BLRM utilizes a small number of network passes to calculate the probability of label noise, thereby improving the accuracy of label refurbishment and providing a reasonable trade-off between computation cost and performance.
